body_en:
Swap a Qin-dynasty peasant with a Qing-dynasty peasant, and both sides slot right in.

The stone mill still turns, the firewood still gets cut, the dry toilet still gets squatted over, the grain still gets handed over. Two thousand years, the same four things. It is absurd when you think about it.

What is more absurd: if they time-traveled to the Song dynasty instead, they would not cope at all.

No travel permit from the village head to leave home, no residence permit to enter the capital — stay a year and you can register as a resident. The Song dynasty, a thousand years ago, was freer than the present day.

Around 2000, back home it still looked the same

No need to go as far back as the Qing. When I was in primary school, around 2000, the way peasants farmed back home — the methods, the tools — had barely changed at all, except for chemical fertilizer.

At spring sowing, one plow, one draft animal, four people: one to drive the animal and hold the plow, one to scatter the seed, one to spread the fertilizer, one to apply the manure. Behind the plow hung a wooden tool for covering the soil — the plow went through, the seed went down, the wood sealed the earth over it. Done.

A Qin peasant dropped into my hometown in 2000 to watch a spring sowing would probably not have found much unfamiliar.

Change came later — and embarrassingly slowly

It was not until I was in high school that animal-drawn seeders started getting cheaper and spreading.

Seed and fertilizer were built into a single tool, hitched behind the plow: the animal pulled, and sowing, fertilizing, and covering the soil happened in one pass. Two workers, freed at a stroke.

Then tractors started getting cheaper too. The animal and the plow were replaced by a tractor pulling a plow-mounted seeder.

I started high school after 2022. In other words, farming only really got its machines in the 2020s — not in some golden age, but once the seeder and the tractor got cheap enough. What changed was not the dynasty. It was the price.

If there is one thing in those two thousand years that beats every dynasty, it is chemical fertilizer.

And the later it got, the worse it could be. In the Qin, forests were everywhere — cut all the firewood you wanted in winter, no fear of the cold. By the Qing, the population had multiplied several times over, the mountains were cut bare, and old photographs show them bald. The climate was colder than in Qin times too. A Qing peasant's life was not necessarily better than a Qin peasant's.

The one real difference: keeping your own profit — and your own losses

Compared with ancient times, the one real difference for a peasant around 2000 was this: you kept your own profit, and bore your own losses.

The land was contracted to your household. A good harvest meant a bit more money; a bad one was yours to absorb. Ancient peasants never had that.

But everything that had to be paid still had to be paid. The agricultural tax. The "three deductions and five charges". Road maintenance fees and vehicle taxes for anyone with a motor vehicle. And at its most absurd, sheep taxed by the head.

The names of the taxes kept changing; the taxes themselves never went away. The agricultural tax ran all the way from the Qin land tax to 2006, when it was finally abolished. A grain tax more than two thousand years old, ended in 2006. The "three deductions and five charges" were abolished in 2002.

One generation walked the whole two thousand years

People born in rural China in the 1960s and 70s spent the first half of their lives in the Qin dynasty and the second half in the postmodern age.

As children they cut pig feed, herded cattle, ate chaff. As adults they use smartphones and drive cars. A road two thousand years never finished, they walked in a single lifetime.

Of course, if you want to be exact, there were differences. Corn and potatoes came from the Americas — no Qin peasant ever ate them — and farm tools changed a few times over. Europe was the same: a Roman farmer and a farmer fourteen hundred years later lived much the same life. Agricultural ages are slow by nature. What finally dragged people out of that loop was not any dynasty — it was the Renaissance and the Industrial Revolution.

So the oil-lamp line cannot be refuted

When a teacher says "without Western civilization, we would still be lighting oil lamps", there is no refuting it.

Without those Western gunboats, the oil lamps would have burned on for at least another half century. Two thousand years of standing still — and still winning every day.

The Forbidden City is magnificent. Tang poetry is magnificent. Peasant life was not magnificent.

Peasant life was the stone mill, firewood, the dry toilet, and the grain tax — two thousand years without moving.
excerpt_en: Stone mills, firewood, dry toilets, and the grain tax: a Qin-dynasty peasant, a late-Qing peasant, and a peasant on the eve of reform lived almost the same life. Two thousand years of 'magnificent' civilization — and the life at the bottom never moved.
title_en: From the Qin Dynasty to the Year 2000, Peasant Life Barely Changed
